title: Der Vogel Greif
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 165. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Swiss German (Alemannic) dialect; the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form. The 1857 edition prints this tale without paragraph breaks; the paragraphing here is editorial, added for readability. The wording is unchanged.
about: KHM 165, printed entirely in Swiss German (Alemannic) dialect, tells of a king whose only daughter can be cured by nothing but a magic apple, promised in marriage to whoever brings her one. Two proud older brothers fail and are sent home in disgrace; it is the youngest, foolish-seeming Hans, who — helped along by a little iron-grey man and eventually the griffin of the title — passes a string of impossible tasks and wins both the cure and the crown. The glossary gives the High German equivalent for every dialect form, since almost none of the tale's vocabulary matches standard spelling.

sentences.t: S isch einisch e Chönig gsi, woner gregiert hat und wiener gheisse hat weiß i nümme.
sentences.l: It has once a king been, how-he ruled and what-he called was know I no-more.
sentences.i: There was once a king, and how he ruled and what he was called I no longer know.
sentences.n: The whole tale is printed in Swiss German (Alemannic), so almost every word looks a little foreign beside the High German of the rest of the collection; the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each form. In the 1857 book the tale stands as a single wall of prose without a break anywhere in it; the divisions between paragraphs here have been added for reading on a screen, and no word of the German has been moved. Here: S isch = es ist, einisch = einmal, e = ein, Chönig = König, gsi = gewesen, woner = wo er (= wie er), gregiert = regiert, wiener = wie er, gheisse = geheißen, weiß i nümme = weiß ich nicht mehr. Two things start at once and never stop: the perfect tense doing the work of the simple past — “ist gewesen” where the north would say “war” — and the Alemannic ch- for High German k-, Chönig for König.

sentences.t: De het kei Sohn gha, nummene einzige Tochter, die isch immer chrank gsi, und kei Dokter het se chönne heile.
sentences.l: He had no son had, only-a single daughter, she has always sick been, and no doctor has her been-able-to heal.
sentences.i: He had no son, only a single daughter, and she was always ill, and no doctor could heal her.
sentences.n: De = der, het = hat, gha = gehabt, nummene = nur eine, chrank = krank, chönne = können, heile = heilen. “het se chönne heile” is the southern perfect with a double infinitive — hat sie heilen können.

sentences.t: Do isch em Chönig profizeit worde si Tochter werd se an Öpfle gsund esse.
sentences.l: Then was to-the king prophesied his daughter would herself on apples well eat.
sentences.i: Then it was prophesied to the king that his daughter would eat herself well on apples.
sentences.n: profizeit worde = prophezeit worden. si Tochter werd se … gsund esse is reported speech with no daß and no verb of saying in front of it: that his daughter would eat herself well. The reflexive “sich gesund essen” — to eat oneself healthy — has no English shape and is kept literal here because the whole plot turns on it.

sentences.t: Do lot er dur sis ganz Land bchant mache wer siner Tochter Öpfel bringe, daß se se gsund dar chönn esse, de müesse zur Frau ha und Chönig wärde.
sentences.l: Then lets he through his whole land known make: whoever to-his daughter apples brings, so that she herself well thereon might eat, he must her to wife have and king become.
sentences.i: Then he had it made known through his whole land that whoever brought his daughter apples, so that she might eat herself well on them, should have her to wife and become king.
sentences.n: lot = lässt, dur = durch, sis = sein, bchant mache = bekannt machen, dar = daran, chönn = könne, de = der, müesse = müsse, ha = haben, wärde = werden. ha is not the laugh “ha” but the plain infinitive haben, and it will keep turning up. The proclamation is the tale’s engine and is repeated almost word for word by each brother.

sentences.t: Das het au ne Pur verno, de drei Söhn gha het.
sentences.l: That has also a farmer heard, who three sons had had.
sentences.i: A farmer heard of this too, one who had three sons.
sentences.n: au = auch — not the cry “ow”; ne Pur = ein Bauer; verno = vernommen, heard, got wind of. Three sons, the youngest slighted: the shape of the tale is set by this one sentence.

sentences.t: Do säit er zum elste „gang ufs Gade ufe, nimm e Chratte (Handkorb) voll vo dene schöne Öpfle mit rothe Bagge und träg se a Hof;
sentences.l: Then says he to-the eldest “go up onto-the loft up, take a basket (hand-basket) full of those fine apples with red cheeks and carry them to court;
sentences.i: Then he said to the eldest: “Go up to the loft, take a basket full of those fine apples with the red cheeks and carry them to court;
sentences.n: The round brackets round (Handkorb) are the Grimms’ own, printed in the 1857 text to gloss the Swiss Chratte for readers outside Switzerland; such brackets are never ours, and there are four more of them in this tale. gang = geh, Gade = Gaden, the upper room or loft where fruit was stored, ufe = hinauf, vo dene = von den, Bagge = Backen, träg = trag, a Hof = an den Hof.

sentences.t: villicht cha se d’ Chönigstochter gsund dra esse und de darfsche hürothe und wirsch Chönig.“
sentences.l: perhaps can herself the king’s-daughter well thereon eat and then may-you-her marry and become king.”
sentences.i: perhaps the king’s daughter can eat herself well on them, and then you may marry her and become king.”
sentences.n: villicht = vielleicht, cha = kann, dra = daran, darfsche = darfst sie (the pronoun swallowed into the verb, which happens all through this tale), hürothe = heiraten, wirsch = wirst.

sentences.t: De Kärle hets e so gmacht und der Weg under d’ Füeß gno.
sentences.l: The fellow has-it thus done and the road under the feet taken.
sentences.i: The lad did so, and took the road under his feet.
sentences.n: Kärle = Kerl, hets = hat es, e so = also, so, gno = genommen. “den Weg unter die Füße nehmen” is to set out on foot — the German picture is of taking the road up underneath you, and it is kept here.

sentences.t: Woner e Zitlang gange gsi isch, begegnet em es chlis isigs Manndle, das frogt ne was er do e dem Chratte häig, do seit der Uele, denn so het er gheisse, „Fröschebäi.“
sentences.l: When-he a while gone been was, meets him a little iron manikin, that asks him what he there in the basket had; then says the Uele, for so was he called, “frogs’ legs.”
sentences.i: When he had gone a while, a little iron manikin met him and asked what he had there in his basket; and Uele — for that was his name — said: “Frogs’ legs.”
sentences.n: woner = wo er, here “als er,” when he; Zitlang = Zeitlang; häig = habe, the subjunctive of reported speech. isig is eisern, of iron: the same word returns for the iron money-chest later in the tale, which is what settles it, though some read it instead as *eisig*, ice-grey. Uele is the Swiss form of Ulrich. The manikin’s question and the answer given to it are the test, and the answer will be repeated twice more.

sentences.t: Das Manndle säit druf „no es sölle si und blibe“ und isch witer gange.
sentences.l: The manikin says thereupon “well, it shall be and remain” and went further.
sentences.i: Thereupon the manikin said: “Well then, so it shall be and so it shall remain,” and went on his way.
sentences.n: druf = darauf; no as an opener is nun, well then; si = sein, to be; blibe = bleiben; witer gange = weitergegangen. “es sölle si und blibe” is the manikin’s whole spell — a wish granted in the shape of a shrug, and the lie the lad told is now the truth in his basket.

sentences.t: Ändle chunt der Uele fürs Schloß un lot se amelde, er hob Öpfel, die d’ Tochter gsund mache, wenn se dervo ässe thue.
sentences.l: At-last comes the Uele before-the castle and has himself announced, he had apples, which the daughter well make, if she of-them eating did.
sentences.i: At last Uele came before the castle and had himself announced: he had apples that would make the daughter well, if she would eat of them.
sentences.n: Ändle = endlich; fürs Schloß = vor das Schloss — Alemannic für regularly does the work of High German vor; lot se amelde = lässt sich anmelden; hob = habe; dervo = davon; “ässe thue” = essen tue, a do-form used as a plain present, common in southern speech.

sentences.t: Das het der Chönig grüsele gfreut und lot der Uele vor se cho, aber, o häie!
sentences.l: That has the king dreadfully pleased and lets the Uele before him come, but, oh dear!
sentences.i: That pleased the king mightily, and he had Uele brought before him — but oh dear!
sentences.n: grüsele is grausam used as an intensifier — dreadfully, mightily — and it is this tale’s favourite word for “very”; gfreut = gefreut. o häie is a cry of dismay, roughly o weh, and the exclamation mark is the 1857 text’s own.

sentences.t: woner ufdeckt, so heter anstatt Öpfel Fröschebäi e dem Chratte, die no zapled händ.
sentences.l: when-he uncovers, so has-he instead-of apples frogs’ legs in the basket, which still wriggled have.
sentences.i: when he uncovered it, he had frogs’ legs in his basket instead of apples, and they were still wriggling.
sentences.n: This sense-unit begins with a small letter in the 1857 printing, which runs it straight on from the cry before it; the wording is untouched. heter = hat er, zapled händ = gezappelt haben. händ is haben, the third person plural, not Hände — one of the places where an Alemannic word looks exactly like a High German one and is not.

sentences.t: Drob isch der Chönig bös worde, und lot ne zum Hus us jage.
sentences.l: Thereat has the king angry become, and lets him to-the house out chase.
sentences.i: At that the king grew angry, and had him chased out of the house.
sentences.n: Drob = darob, at that; bös worde = böse geworden; “zum Hus us jage” = zum Haus hinausjagen, the particle us (aus) sitting after the noun as southern speech likes it. us is aus here, not uns.

sentences.t: Woner häi cho isch, so verzelter dem Ätte wies em gange isch.
sentences.l: When-he home come was, so tells-he to-the father how-it him gone is.
sentences.i: When he came home he told his father how it had gone with him.
sentences.n: häi = heim; verzelter = verzählt er, that is erzählt er; Ätte is the Swiss word for father, the one this tale uses throughout; “wies em gange isch” = wie es ihm gegangen ist.

sentences.t: Do schickt der Ätte der noelst Son, de Säme gheisse het; aber dem isch es ganz glich gange wie im Uele.
sentences.l: Then sends the father the next son, who Säme called was; but to-him has it quite the-same gone as to-the Uele.
sentences.i: Then the father sent the next son, who was called Säme; but it went with him exactly as it had with Uele.
sentences.n: noelst = nächst, the next in age; Säme is the Swiss form of Samuel. glich here is gleich, the same — not the verb gleichen; “im Uele” is dem Uele, with the southern article im for dem.

sentences.t: Es isch em halt au es chlis isigs Manndle begegnet und das het ne gfrogt was er do e dem Chratte häig,
sentences.l: It has him just also a little iron manikin met and that has him asked what he there in the basket had,
sentences.i: A little iron manikin met him too, and asked him what he had there in his basket,
sentences.n: halt is the southern particle of resignation — just, simply — and it has no English word of its own; it recurs through the tale and is carried by a light “just.” frogt/gfrogt = fragt/gefragt.

sentences.t: der Säme säit „Seüborst,“ und das isigs Manndle säit „no es söll si und blibe.“
sentences.l: the Säme says “pig’s bristles,” and the iron manikin says “well, it shall be and remain.”
sentences.i: and Säme said: “Pig’s bristles,” and the iron manikin said: “Well then, so it shall be and so it shall remain.”
sentences.n: Seüborst = Sauborsten, the coarse bristles of a pig, used for brushes and by cobblers as a needle. The second brother lies as the first did, and the spell is spoken again in the same words.

sentences.t: Woner do vor es Chönigsschloß cho isch, und säit er heb Öpfel, a dene se d’ Chönigstochter gsund chönn esse,
sentences.l: When-he then before a king’s-castle come was, and says he had apples, on which the king’s-daughter well could eat,
sentences.i: When he came before the king’s castle and said he had apples that the king’s daughter could eat herself well on,
sentences.n: es Chönigsschloß = ein Königsschloss; a dene = an denen; heb = habe, the subjunctive of reported speech again — the tale keeps the brothers’ claims at arm’s length in this way, and the reader can hear that nobody quite believes them.

sentences.t: so händ se ne nid welle ine lo, und händ gsäit es sig scho eine do gsi und heb se füre Nare gha.
sentences.l: so have they him not wanted in let, and have said there be already one there been and had them for-a fool held.
sentences.i: they would not let him in, and said there had already been one there who had made fools of them.
sentences.n: “händ se ne nid welle ine lo” = haben sie ihn nicht wollen hinein lassen — a chain of three infinitives, the southern perfect with a double infinitive, and welle here is wollen, not eine Welle. ine = hinein. “für einen Narren haben” is to take somebody for a fool, to make a fool of them.

sentences.t: Der Säme het aber aghalte, er heb gwüß dere Öpfel, se solle ne nume ine lo.
sentences.l: The Säme has however insisted, he had for-certain such apples, they should him only in let.
sentences.i: But Säme kept at it: he certainly had such apples, they need only let him in.
sentences.n: aghalte = angehalten, kept on, pressed; gwüß = gewiss; dere Öpfel = derer Äpfel, apples of that kind; nume = nur.

sentences.t: Ändle händ sem glaubt, und füre ne vor der Chönig.
sentences.l: At-last have they-him believed, and led him before the king.
sentences.i: At last they believed him, and led him before the king.
sentences.n: sem = sie ihm, two pronouns run together into one word. füre here is führen, they led — not für and not the hervor that the same spelling carries elsewhere in this tale; the glossary entry sets out all three.

sentences.t: Aber woner er si Chratte ufdeckt, so het er halt Seüborst.
sentences.l: But when-he he his basket uncovers, so has he just pig’s bristles.
sentences.i: But when he uncovered his basket, all he had was pig’s bristles.
sentences.n: “woner er” prints the pronoun twice — woner is already wo er — and the 1857 text keeps the slip; it is left standing here. si Chratte = sein Korb.

sentences.t: Das het der Chönig gar schröckele erzürnt, so daß er der Säme us em Hus het lo peütsche.
sentences.l: That has the king quite frightfully angered, so that he the Säme out of-the house had let whip.
sentences.i: That angered the king so frightfully that he had Säme whipped out of the house.
sentences.n: gar is the intensifier quite, thoroughly, not gar nicht; schröckele = schrecklich; peütsche = peitschen, to whip. The 1857 text does not soften this, and neither does the English.

sentences.t: Woner häi cho isch, so het er gsäit wies em gange isch.
sentences.l: When-he home come was, so has he said how-it him gone is.
sentences.i: When he came home he told how it had gone with him.
sentences.n: The same sentence that closed the first brother’s journey, repeated almost word for word to close the second — the tale keeps its three attempts in step, and only the third will break the pattern.

sentences.t: Do chunt der jüngst Bueb, dem händse nume der dumm Hans gsäit, und frogt der Ätte ob er au mit Öpfel goh dörf.
sentences.l: Then comes the youngest lad, to-whom they-had only “the stupid Hans” said, and asks the father whether he also with apples go may.
sentences.i: Then came the youngest lad, whom they called nothing but stupid Hans, and he asked his father whether he might go with apples too.
sentences.n: chunt = kommt; Bueb = Bube, lad; “dem händse nume der dumm Hans gsäit” = dem haben sie nur der dumme Hans gesagt — the person called is in the dative and the name stays in the nominative, which is how German names a nickname. goh = gehen, dörf = darf.

sentences.t: „Jo,“ säit do der Ätte, „du wärst der rächt Kerle derzue, wenn die gschite nüt usrichte, was wettest denn du usrichte.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” says then the father, “you would-be the right fellow for-it; if the clever ones nothing accomplish, what would you accomplish.”
sentences.i: “Oh yes,” said the father, “you would be just the man for it; if the clever ones can do nothing, what would you do?”
sentences.n: Jo = ja, and it is heavy with irony here. rächt = recht; Kerle is the singular Kerl with the -e the south adds; derzue = dazu; gschite = Gescheiten; nüt = nichts; usrichte = ausrichten, to accomplish; wettest = wolltest. The 1857 text ends the question with a full stop, not a question mark, and that is left as it stands.

sentences.t: Der Bueb het aber nit no glo: „e woll, Ätte, i will au goh.“
sentences.l: The lad has however not let-up: “oh yes, father, I want also to-go.”
sentences.i: But the lad would not let it alone: “Oh yes I will, father, I want to go too.”
sentences.n: “nit no glo” = nicht nachgelassen, did not give over — no here is nach, not noch, and the same little word does duty for both all through the tale. e woll = ei wohl, a stubborn oh yes. i is ich, not the interjection ei.

sentences.t: „Gang mer doch ewäg, du dumme Kerle, du muest warte bis gschiter wirsch“ säit druf der Ätte und chert em der Rügge.
sentences.l: “Go me though away, you stupid fellow, you must wait until cleverer you-become” says thereupon the father and turns him the back.
sentences.i: “Get away with you, you stupid fellow, you must wait until you grow cleverer,” said the father, and turned his back on him.
sentences.n: “gang mer doch ewäg” = geh mir doch weg — the mer is the dative of interest, mir, which English drops. muest = musst, gschiter = gescheiter, wirsch = wirst, chert em der Rügge = kehrt ihm den Rücken.

sentences.t: Der Hans aber zupft ne hinde am Chittel „e woll, Ätte, i will au goh.“
sentences.l: The Hans however plucks him behind at-the coat “oh yes, father, I want also to-go.”
sentences.i: But Hans plucked at the back of his coat: “Oh yes I will, father, I want to go too.”
sentences.n: zupft ne = zupft ihn; hinde = hinten; Chittel = Kittel, the smock or coat of a working man. The boy’s one line is printed twice, unchanged, and the repetition is the joke.

sentences.t: „No minetwäge, so gang, de wirsch woll wieder ome cho“ gitt der Ätte zur Antwort eme nidige Ton.
sentences.l: “Well for-my-part, so go, you will surely again back come” gives the father as answer in-a spiteful tone.
sentences.i: “Well, for all I care, go then — you will be back soon enough,” the father answered in a spiteful tone.
sentences.n: minetwäge = meinetwegen; gitt = gibt; “wieder ome cho” = wieder zurückkommen, to come back again — ome is the Alemannic ume, back; nidig = neidisch, gehässig, spiteful. woll is wohl, the particle of grim confidence — you’ll be back right enough.

sentences.t: Der Bueb hat se aber grüsele gfreut und isch ufgumpet.
sentences.l: The lad has himself however dreadfully rejoiced and is up-jumped.
sentences.i: But the lad was mightily pleased, and jumped for joy.
sentences.n: se = sich; ufgumpet = aufgehüpft, from gumpen, to hop or leap, a thoroughly southern word. grüsele, this tale’s word for “very,” is doing its work again.

sentences.t: „Jo, thue jetz no wiene Nar, du wirsch vo äim Tag zum andere no dümmer“ säit der Ätte wieder.
sentences.l: “Yes, do now still like-a fool, you will from one day to-the other still stupider” says the father again.
sentences.i: “Yes, go on playing the fool — you grow stupider from one day to the next,” said the father again.
sentences.n: wiene = wie ein; Nar = Narr; äim = einem; dümmer = dümmer. The verb of the second clause is left out — “du wirst … no dümmer” with no werden-participle — and it is left out in the English too.

sentences.t: Dat het aber im Hans nüt gmacht und het se e siner Freud nid lo störe.
sentences.l: That has however to-the Hans nothing done and has himself in his joy not let disturb.
sentences.i: But that meant nothing to Hans, and he would not let his joy be disturbed.
sentences.n: Dat is das — an odd spelling for this tale, which everywhere else writes das, and it occurs only twice. im Hans = dem Hans; e siner Freud = in seiner Freude; “nid lo störe” = nicht stören lassen.

sentences.t: Wils aber gli Nacht gsi isch, so het er dänkt er well warte bis am Morge, er möcht hüt doch nümme na Hof gcho.
sentences.l: Because it however soon night been was, so has he thought he would wait until the morning, he might today anyway no-more to court come.
sentences.i: But because night was coming on, he thought he would wait until morning; he could hardly reach the court that day in any case.
sentences.n: Wils = weil es; gli = gleich, here soon; well = wolle; nümme = nicht mehr; na Hof = nach Hof; gcho = gekommen. The reported thought runs on with no daß, and the subjunctive well and möcht carry it.

sentences.t: Z’ Nacht im Bett het er nid chönne schloffe,
sentences.l: At night in bed has he not been-able-to sleep,
sentences.i: That night in bed he could not sleep,
sentences.n: Z’ Nacht = zu Nacht, at night; “het er nid chönne schloffe” = hat er nicht schlafen können, the double infinitive again; schloffe = schlafen.

sentences.t: und wenn er au ne ihli igschlummert isch, so hets em traumt vo schöne Jumpfere, vo Schlößern, Gold und Silber und allerhand dere Sache meh.
sentences.l: and when he indeed a little-while dozed-off was, so has-it him dreamed of fine maidens, of castles, gold and silver and all sorts of-such things more.
sentences.i: and even when he did doze off for a little, he dreamed of fine maidens, of castles, of gold and silver and all manner of such things.
sentences.n: ne ihli = ein Weilchen; igschlummert = eingeschlummert; “hets em traumt” = hat es ihm geträumt, the impersonal dream-construction German uses — it dreamed to him; Jumpfere = Jungfern; Schlößern = Schlössern; “dere Sache meh” = solcher Sachen mehr. meh here is mehr, not a goat’s bleat.

sentences.t: Am Morge früe macht er se up der Wäg,
sentences.l: In-the morning early makes he himself onto the road,
sentences.i: Early in the morning he set out,
sentences.n: up is the same word as uf, auf; “macht er se uf der Wäg” = macht er sich auf den Weg. The third journey begins exactly as the other two did, and the reader is meant to hear it.

sentences.t: und gli drufe bchuntem es chlis mutzigs Manndle, eme isige Chläidle, und frogt ne was er do e dem Chratte häig.
sentences.l: and soon thereupon meets-him a little stumpy manikin, in-a iron little-coat, and asks him what he there in the basket had.
sentences.i: and soon after, a little stumpy manikin in an iron coat met him and asked what he had there in his basket.
sentences.n: bchuntem = bekommt ihm, in the older sense of jemandem bekommen, to meet somebody — not to receive; drufe = darauf; mutzig is stumpy, dumpy; Chläidle = Kleidchen. It is the same manikin as before, though the tale describes him afresh.

sentences.t: Der Hans gitt em zur Antwort er heb Öpfel, a dene d’ Chönigstochter se gsund äße sött.
sentences.l: The Hans gives him as answer he had apples, on which the king’s-daughter herself well eat should.
sentences.i: Hans answered that he had apples on which the king’s daughter was to eat herself well.
sentences.n: gitt = gibt; heb = habe; äße = essen; sött = sollte. Hans tells the truth where his brothers lied, and the whole tale turns on that and on nothing else.

sentences.t: „No,“ säit das Manndle, „es sölle söttige (solche) si und blibe.“
sentences.l: “Well,” says the manikin, “it shall such-ones (such) be and remain.”
sentences.i: “Well then,” said the manikin, “so let them be and so let them remain.”
sentences.n: The round brackets round (solche) are the Grimms’ own, glossing the Swiss söttige for their readers. The spell is spoken for the third time in the same words — and this time it confirms a truth instead of fixing a lie.

sentences.t: Aber am Hof händ se der Hans partu nit welle ine lo,
sentences.l: But at-the court have they the Hans absolutely not wanted in let,
sentences.i: But at the court they absolutely would not let Hans in,
sentences.n: partu is the French partout worn down into dialect — absolutely, on no account; it is the kind of word that came into Swiss speech with mercenary service abroad. welle = wollen, ine lo = hinein lassen.

sentences.t: denn es sige scho zwee do gsi und hebe gsäit se bringe Öpfel und do heb äine Fröschebäi und der ander Seüborst gha.
sentences.l: for there had already two there been and had said they bring apples and then had one frogs’ legs and the other pig’s bristles had.
sentences.i: for two had already been there, they said, who claimed to be bringing apples, and one had had frogs’ legs and the other pig’s bristles.
sentences.n: sige, hebe, heb are all subjunctives of reported speech — the gate-keepers are quoting themselves, and German marks that with the verb alone; zwee = zwei; do = da; äine = einer; der ander = der andere.

sentences.t: Der Hans het aber gar grüsele aghalte, er heb gwöß kene Fröschebäi, sondern von de schönste Öpfle, die im ganze Chönigreich wachse.
sentences.l: The Hans has however quite dreadfully insisted, he had for-certain no frogs’ legs, but rather of the finest apples that in-the whole kingdom grow.
sentences.i: But Hans pressed them hard: he certainly had no frogs’ legs, but the finest apples that grew in the whole kingdom.
sentences.n: gwöß is the same word as gwüß, gewiss, spelled differently a few lines apart — the 1857 text is not consistent and is not made consistent here. kene = keine; Chönigreich = Königreich; wachse = wachsen.

sentences.t: Woner de so ordele gredt het, so dänke d’ Thörhüeter de chönn nid lüge und lönde ine,
sentences.l: When-he then so properly spoken had, so think the gate-keepers he could not lie and let-him in,
sentences.i: When he had spoken so properly, the gate-keepers thought that this one could not be lying, and let him in,
sentences.n: ordele = ordentlich; gredt = geredet; Thörhüeter = Torhüter, with the 1857 spelling Thör for Tür; lönde = lassen, third person plural. The tale gives the porters the judgment, and it is the honest speech and not the apples that persuades them.

sentences.t: und se händ au rächt gha, denn wo der Hans si Chratte vor em Chönig abdeckt, so sind goldgäle Öpfel füre cho.
sentences.l: and they have also right had, for when the Hans his basket before the king uncovers, so are golden-yellow apples forth come.
sentences.i: and they were right, too, for when Hans uncovered his basket before the king, out came golden-yellow apples.
sentences.n: wo here is als, when — the temporal use that this tale prefers to wenn; “rächt gha” = recht gehabt; goldgäle = goldgelbe; “füre cho” = hervorgekommen. füre is hervor here; a few lines back the same spelling was führen, and later it is für — the glossary sets out all three.

sentences.t: De Chönig het se gfreut und lot gli der Tochter dervo bringe, und wartet jetz e banger Erwartig bis menem der Bericht bringt, was se für Würkig tho hebe.
sentences.l: The king has himself rejoiced and has at-once to-the daughter of-them brought, and waits now in anxious expectation until one him the report brings, what they for effect done have.
sentences.i: The king rejoiced, and had some brought to his daughter at once, and now waited in anxious expectation until word should be brought him of what effect they had had.
sentences.n: “het se gfreut” = hat sich gefreut; menem = man ihm; Erwartig = Erwartung; Würkig = Wirkung; “tho hebe” = getan haben. e banger Erwartig stands without a preposition where High German would say in banger Erwartung.

sentences.t: Aber nid lange Zit vergot, so bringt em öpper Bricht: aber was meineder wer isch das gsi?
sentences.l: But not long time passes, so brings him somebody news: but what think-you who has that been?
sentences.i: Not much time passed before somebody brought him word — and who do you think it was?
sentences.n: vergot = vergeht; öpper = jemand, somebody; Bricht = Bericht, spelled short here and full a line earlier. meineder = meint ihr — the teller turns and addresses the listeners directly, one of the few places where the voice of the person who told this tale is audible.

sentences.t: d’ Tochter selber isch es gsi.
sentences.l: the daughter herself has it been.
sentences.i: It was the daughter herself.
sentences.n: This sense-unit begins with a small letter in the 1857 printing, which runs it on from the question before it as one breath; the wording is untouched.

sentences.t: So bald se vo dene Öpfle ggäße gha het, isch e gsund us em Bett gsprunge.
sentences.l: As soon-as she of those apples eaten had had, is she well out of the bed sprung.
sentences.i: As soon as she had eaten of those apples she sprang out of bed well again.
sentences.n: “ggäße gha het” = gegessen gehabt hat, a double perfect the south uses where High German is content with one; e here is the pronoun sie, she — the same spelling that elsewhere in this tale is ein and in. gsprunge = gesprungen.

sentences.t: Wie der Chönig e Freud gha het, chame nid beschribe.
sentences.l: What the king a joy had had, can-one not describe.
sentences.i: What joy the king had is not to be described.
sentences.n: chame = kann man; beschribe = beschreiben. Wie … e Freud is an exclamation used as an object clause — what a joy — and it needs no question word in German.

sentences.t: Aber jetz het er d’ Tochter dem Hans nid welle zur Frau ge
sentences.l: But now has he the daughter to-the Hans not wanted to wife give
sentences.i: But now he would not give the daughter to Hans to wife after all,
sentences.n: “het er … nid welle … ge” = hat er nicht geben wollen, the double infinitive once more. The king breaks his own proclamation here, and will break it twice more: the promise, and then a task instead of the promise, is this tale’s pattern.

sentences.t: un säit er müeß em zerst none Wäidlig (Nachen) mache, de ufem drochne Land wäidliger geu as im Wasser.
sentences.l: and says he must him first still-a skiff (boat) make, which on-the dry land more-swiftly went than in-the water.
sentences.i: and said he must first make him a skiff that would go faster on dry land than in the water.
sentences.n: The round brackets round (Nachen) are the Grimms’ own, glossing the Swiss Wäidlig — the flat-bottomed boat of the Rhine and the Swiss lakes — for readers who would not know it. The joke of the task is in the word: wäidlig the boat, wäidliger the comparative of wäidlich, swiftly, briskly, so that the sentence sounds like “a skiff that goes skiffier on land than on the water,” and no English word does both jobs. none = noch ein; geu = gehe; as = als.

sentences.t: Der Hans nimmt de Betingig a und got häi und verzelts wies eme gangen seig.
sentences.l: The Hans takes the condition on and goes home and tells-it how-it him gone be.
sentences.i: Hans accepted the condition, went home, and told how it had gone with him.
sentences.n: “nimmt … a” = nimmt an, the particle standing at the end where German leaves it; Betingig = Bedingung; got = geht; seig = sei, the subjunctive of reported speech.

sentences.t: Do schickt der Ätte der Uele is Holz um e söttige Wäidlig z’ mache.
sentences.l: Then sends the father the Uele into-the wood in-order-to a such skiff to make.
sentences.i: Then the father sent Uele into the wood to make such a skiff.
sentences.n: is Holz = ins Holz; söttige = solchen; “z’ mache” = zu machen. The three-brother pattern starts over from the beginning, and the reader now knows what will happen twice before it goes right.

sentences.t: Er hat flißig gewärret (gearbeitet) und derzue gpfiffe.
sentences.l: He has diligently worked (worked) and thereto whistled.
sentences.i: He worked away diligently, and whistled as he went.
sentences.n: The round brackets round (gearbeitet) are the Grimms’ own: gewärret is a Swiss word for working away at something, and they gloss it for their readers. flißig = fleißig; gpfiffe = gepfiffen.

sentences.t: Z’ Mittag, wo d’ Sunne am höchste gstande isch, chunt es chlis isigs Manndle und frogt was er do mach.
sentences.l: At midday, when the sun at-the highest stood, comes a little iron manikin and asks what he there was-doing.
sentences.i: At midday, when the sun stood at its highest, a little iron manikin came and asked what he was doing there.
sentences.n: wo is als, when — the temporal use again; gstande = gestanden; mach = mache, the subjunctive of the reported question. Everything is as it was with the apples: same manikin, same question, and the same chance to answer it honestly.

sentences.t: Der Uele gitt em zur Antwort „Chelle (hölzernes Geräth).“
sentences.l: The Uele gives him as answer “ladles (wooden implement).”
sentences.i: Uele answered: “Ladles.”
sentences.n: The round brackets round (hölzernes Geräth) are the Grimms’ own gloss on Chelle — Kellen, the big wooden ladles and scoops of a farm kitchen. Geräth is the 1857 spelling of Gerät.

sentences.t: Das isig Männdle säit „no es sölle si und blibe.“
sentences.l: The iron manikin says “well, it shall be and remain.”
sentences.i: The iron manikin said: “Well then, so it shall be and so it shall remain.”
sentences.n: Männdle is spelled with a double n here and single n everywhere else — the 1857 text varies and is left as it stands.

sentences.t: Z’ Obe meint der Uele er heb jetz e Wäidlig gmacht, aber woner het welle isitze, so sinds alles Chelle gsi.
sentences.l: In-the evening thinks the Uele he had now a skiff made, but when-he had wanted in-to-sit, so were-they all ladles been.
sentences.i: In the evening Uele thought he had made a skiff, but when he went to sit himself in it, it was all ladles.
sentences.n: Z’ Obe = zu Abend, in the evening — Obe is Abend, not aber. “woner het welle isitze” = wo er hat einsitzen wollen; sinds = sind es.

sentences.t: Der anner Tag got der Säme e Wald, aber s’ isch em ganz gliche gange wie im Uele.
sentences.l: The other day goes the Säme into-the wood, but it has him quite the-same gone as to-the Uele.
sentences.i: The next day Säme went into the wood, but it went with him exactly as it had with Uele.
sentences.n: anner = ander; e Wald = in den Wald — e is in here, the same spelling that elsewhere is ein and sie. gliche is gleich, the same, not a form of gleichen.

sentences.t: Am dritte Tag got der dumm Hans.
sentences.l: On-the third day goes the stupid Hans.
sentences.i: On the third day stupid Hans went.
sentences.n: Seven words, where each older brother’s attempt took several sentences: the tale changes key by going short, and the paragraph here begins with that change. dritte = dritte, and got = geht.

sentences.t: Er schafft rächt flißig, daß es im ganze Wald tönt vo sine chräftige Schläge, derzue singt er und pfift er rächt lustig.
sentences.l: He works right diligently, so-that it in-the whole wood rings from his powerful blows, thereto sings he and whistles he right merrily.
sentences.i: He worked away with a will, so that the whole wood rang with his powerful blows, and sang and whistled merrily as he worked.
sentences.n: schafft is schaffen in its southern sense of working, labouring — not the High German schaffen, to create or to get rid of. tönt = tönt, rings; chräftige = kräftigen; pfift = pfeift.

sentences.t: Da chunt wieder das chli Manndle z’ Mittag, wos am heißeste gsi isch, und frogt was er do mach.
sentences.l: There comes again the little manikin at midday, when-it at-the hottest been was, and asks what he there was-doing.
sentences.i: At midday, when the heat was at its worst, the little manikin came again and asked what he was doing there.
sentences.n: wos = wo es, that is als es; heißeste = heißesten. The manikin comes at the hour when a man is most likely to answer shortly and badly, and that is the third time it has done so.

sentences.t: „E Wäidlig, de uf em drochne Land wäidliger got as uf em Wasser,“ un wenn er dermit fertig seig, so chom er d’ Chönigstochter zur Frau über.
sentences.l: “A skiff, which on the dry land more-swiftly goes than on the water,” and when he therewith finished be, so came he the king’s-daughter to wife over.
sentences.i: “A skiff that goes faster on dry land than on the water” — and when he had finished it, he would get the king’s daughter to wife.
sentences.n: Hans answers with the task word for word, as he answered with the apples. dermit = damit; seig = sei; “chom er … über” = überkomme er, he would get her — überkommen, to come by a thing, is separable and its particle über is standing at the end.

sentences.t: „No,“ säit das Manndle, „es söll e so äine ge und blibe.“
sentences.l: “Well,” says the manikin, “it shall a such-one be-given and remain.”
sentences.i: “Well then,” said the manikin, “let there be such a one, and let it remain so.”
sentences.n: “e so äine” = ein so einer, one of that sort. ge is geben; the spell has the same shape as before but now grants what was honestly named.

sentences.t: Z’ Obe, wo d’ Sunne aber z’ Gold gange isch, isch der Hans au fertig gsi mit sim Wäidlig und Schiff und Gscher.
sentences.l: In-the evening, when the sun however to gold gone was, was the Hans also finished with his skiff and ship and gear.
sentences.i: In the evening, when the sun had turned to gold, Hans too was finished, with his skiff and ship and tackle.
sentences.n: “z’ Gold gange” — gone to gold — is the tale’s one piece of description, and it is kept as it stands rather than smoothed into “set.” “mit Schiff und Gscher” = mit Schiff und Geschirr is a set phrase meaning with everything belonging to it, lock, stock and barrel. sim = seinem.

sentences.t: Er sitzt i und ruederet der Residenz zue.
sentences.l: He sits in and rows the residence toward.
sentences.i: He seated himself in it and rowed toward the royal town.
sentences.n: “sitzt i” = sitzt ein, gets in and sits down, with the particle i (ein) after the verb; “ruederet der Residenz zue” = rudert der Residenz zu, again with the particle at the end. Die Residenz is the town where the ruler resides — the capital.

sentences.t: Der Wäidlig isch aber so gschwind gange wie der Wind.
sentences.l: The skiff is however so swift gone as the wind.
sentences.i: And the skiff went as swift as the wind.
sentences.n: gschwind = geschwind. The boat is on dry land and nobody remarks on it — the tale does not stop to be amazed by its own marvels, which is one of the ways it differs from a literary fairy tale.

sentences.t: Der Chönig hets von witen gseh, will aber im Hans si Tochter nonig ge
sentences.l: The king has-it from far seen, wants however to-the Hans his daughter still-not give
sentences.i: The king saw it from far off, but still would not give Hans his daughter,
sentences.n: hets = hat es; von witen = von weitem; gseh = gesehen; nonig = noch nicht. Third promise, third refusal.

sentences.t: und säit er müeß zerst no hundert Haase hüete vom Morge früeh bis z’ Obe spot, und wenn em äine furt chömm, so chömm er d’ Tochter nit über.
sentences.l: and says he must first still a-hundred hares herd from-the morning early until in-the evening late, and if him one away came, so came he the daughter not over.
sentences.i: and said he must first herd a hundred hares from early morning till late evening, and if a single one got away from him he should not have the daughter.
sentences.n: Haase = Hasen; hüete = hüten, to herd or keep watch over; spot = spät; chömm = käme, twice, the subjunctive carrying the king’s condition; “chömm er d’ Tochter nit über” = überkäme er die Tochter nicht. Herding hares — animals that exist to run away — is the impossible task in its purest form.

sentences.t: Der Hans isch e des z’ friede gsi,
sentences.l: The Hans was in that content,
sentences.i: Hans was content with that,
sentences.n: “e des z’ friede” = in dem zufrieden; friede here is part of zufrieden and is not der Friede, peace.

sentences.t: und gli am andere Tag got er mit siner Heerd uf d’ Wäid und paßt verwändt uf daß em keine dervo laufe.
sentences.l: and soon on-the next day goes he with his herd onto the pasture and watches unwaveringly out that him none of-them run.
sentences.i: and early the next day he went out with his herd to the pasture, and kept an unwavering watch that none of them should run off.
sentences.n: Heerd = Herde, a herd — of hares; Wäid = Weide; “paßt … uf” = passt auf, with the particle uf held back to the end; verwändt = unverwandt, without turning the eyes away; dervo laufe = davonlaufen.

sentences.t: Nid mänge Stund isch vergange, so chunt e Magd vom Schloß und säit zum Hans er söll ere gschwind e Haas ge, so hebe Wisite über cho.
sentences.l: Not many an-hour is passed, so comes a maid from-the castle and says to-the Hans he should her quickly a hare give, they-had visitors over come.
sentences.i: Not many hours had passed before a maid came from the castle and told Hans he should quickly give her a hare — they had visitors.
sentences.n: mänge = manche; “hebe Wisite über cho” = hätten Visite überkommen, they had got visitors; Wisite is the French visite, which came into Swiss speech as it did into the German of the whole south. The king is testing him by a trick now instead of a task.

sentences.t: Der Hans hett aber woll gemerkt wo das use will und säit er gäb e keine, der Chönig chön denn morn siner Wisite mit Haasepfäffer ufwarte.
sentences.l: The Hans has however surely noticed where that out wants and says he gave none, the king could then tomorrow his visitors with hare-pepper serve.
sentences.i: But Hans saw well enough what that was driving at, and said he would give none: the king might wait till tomorrow to serve his visitors jugged hare.
sentences.n: “wo das use will” = wo das hinaus will, what it is driving at; gäb = gäbe and chön = könne are subjunctives of reported speech; morn = morgen; Haasepfäffer = Hasenpfeffer, hare stewed in a dark peppery sauce; ufwarte = aufwarten, to wait on a guest with a dish.

sentences.t: D’ Magd het aber nid no glo und am Änd fot so no a resniere.
sentences.l: The maid has however not let-up and at-the end begins she even to argue.
sentences.i: But the maid would not let it alone, and in the end she even began to argue.
sentences.n: “nid no glo” = nicht nachgelassen, as with the boy and his father earlier; Änd = Ende; “fot … a” = fängt an, the particle a (an) held to the end; resniere = räsonieren, to hold forth, to argue back. The so before no is standing for sie, she — the tale writes both so and sö for both words, and the sense has to decide.

sentences.t: Do säit der Hans wenn d’ Chönigstochter selber chömm, so woll er ene Haas ge.
sentences.l: Then says the Hans if the king’s-daughter herself came, so would he a hare give.
sentences.i: Then Hans said that if the king’s daughter came herself, he would give a hare.
sentences.n: chömm = käme, woll = wolle: two subjunctives carrying the condition. Hans has understood the trap and sets one of his own.

sentences.t: Dat het d’ Magd im Schloß gsäit, und d’ Tochter isch selber gange.
sentences.l: That has the maid in-the castle said, and the daughter is herself gone.
sentences.i: The maid said so at the castle, and the daughter went herself.
sentences.n: Dat for das, the second and last of the two odd spellings; the tale writes das everywhere else. selber = selber, herself.

sentences.t: Underdesse isch aber zum Hans das chli Manndle wieder cho und frogt der Hans was er do thüej.
sentences.l: Meanwhile is however to the Hans the little manikin again come and asks the Hans what he there was-doing.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the little manikin had come to Hans again, and asked him what he was doing there.
sentences.n: Underdesse = unterdessen; thüej = tue, the subjunctive of the reported question. The manikin arrives a third time, and a third time asks the same question.

sentences.t: „He, do müeß er hundert Haase hüete, daß em kaine dervo lauf, und denn dörf er d’ Chönigstochter hürothe und wäre Chönig.“
sentences.l: “Well, there must he a-hundred hares herd, so that him none of-them run, and then may he the king’s-daughter marry and become king.”
sentences.i: “Well, he has to herd a hundred hares here so that none of them runs off, and then he may marry the king’s daughter and become king.”
sentences.n: Hans is answering about himself, and yet the speech runs in the third person and in the subjunctive — müeß, lauf, dörf — as though somebody else were reporting it. The 1857 text slides between quoted and reported speech like this more than once, and the English keeps the slide rather than tidying it. wäre here is werden, to become, not a form of sein.

sentences.t: „Guet,“ säit das Manndle, „do hesch es Pfifle, und wenn der äine furtlauft, so pfif nume, denn chunt er wieder ume.“
sentences.l: “Good,” says the manikin, “there have-you a little-pipe, and when you-one away-runs, so whistle only, then comes he again back.”
sentences.i: “Good,” said the manikin, “here you have a little pipe, and when one runs off from you, just whistle, and back he comes.”
sentences.n: hesch = hast; Pfifle = Pfeifchen, a little whistle; “der äine” = dir einer, the dative of the person it happens to; pfif = pfeif; nume = nur; ume = wieder um, back. This is the fourth gift of the manikin and the only one he hands over.

sentences.t: Wo do d’ Tochter cho isch, so gitt ere der Hans e Haas is Fürtüchle.
sentences.l: When then the daughter come was, so gives her the Hans a hare into-the little-apron.
sentences.i: When the daughter came, Hans gave her a hare into her apron.
sentences.n: ere = ihr; Fürtüchle = Fürtüchlein, from Fürtuch, the southern word for an apron — literally a fore-cloth. The king’s daughter carrying off a live hare in her apron is the whole picture.

sentences.t: Aber wo se öppe hundert Schritt wit gsi isch, so pfift der Hans,
sentences.l: But when she about a-hundred paces far been was, so whistles the Hans,
sentences.i: But when she was about a hundred paces off, Hans whistled,
sentences.n: öppe = etwa, about; wit = weit. The trap shuts exactly at the distance from which she cannot get back in time.

sentences.t: und de Haas springt ere us em Schäubele use und, was gisch was hesch, wieder zu der Heerd.
sentences.l: and the hare springs her out of the little-gown out and, what give-you what have-you, again to the herd.
sentences.i: and the hare sprang out of her gown and away, as fast as ever it could, back to the herd.
sentences.n: “was gisch was hesch” — literally what do you give, what do you have — is a set southern phrase for headlong speed, and there is no English idiom that matches it, so the sense is given plainly here and the German picture left in this note. Schäubele is a little Schaube, a loose over-gown; the word is rare and the exact garment is not certain.

sentences.t: Wo’s Obe gsi isch, so pfift de Haasehirt no emol und luegt ob alle do sige und treibt se do zum Schloß.
sentences.l: When-it evening been was, so whistles the hare-herd once more and looks whether all there be and drives them then to-the castle.
sentences.i: When evening came the hare-herd whistled once more, looked whether they were all there, and drove them to the castle.
sentences.n: Wo’s = wo es, als es; Haasehirt = Hasenhirt, hare-herd — a word the tale coins on the spot, as one says Kuhhirt; luegt = schaut, looks; sige = seien.

sentences.t: Der Chönig het se verwunderet wie au der Hans im Stand gsi seig hundert Haase z’ hüete, daß em käine dervo glofe isch;
sentences.l: The king has himself wondered how indeed the Hans in-the state been be a-hundred hares to herd, so that him none of-them run away is;
sentences.i: The king wondered how Hans could have been able to herd a hundred hares without one running away from him;
sentences.n: “im Stand si” = imstande sein, to be able; “gsi seig” = gewesen sei; glofe = gelaufen. Stand here is the noun der Stand, not a past tense of stehen.

sentences.t: er will em aber d’ Tochter äine weg nonig ge, und säit er müß em no ne Fädere us d’ Vogelgrife Stehl bringe.
sentences.l: he wants him however the daughter one way still-not give, and says he must him yet a feather out-of the Vogel Greif’s tail bring.
sentences.i: but he would not give him the daughter all the same, and said he must bring him a feather out of the Vogel Greif’s tail.
sentences.n: “äine weg” is einerweg, all the same, in any case — the sense is clear enough from the sentence, though the phrase is not one this collection uses elsewhere and the reading is not certain. der Vogel Greif is the griffin, the eagle-lion of old bestiaries; the name is left standing in German, as the tale’s title leaves it. Stehl is the tail, and the fourth task is now a journey rather than a piece of work.

sentences.t: Der Hans macht se grad uf der Wäg und marschiert rächt handle vorwärts.
sentences.l: The Hans makes himself straight onto the road and marches right briskly forward.
sentences.i: Hans set out at once, and marched briskly on his way.
sentences.n: grad = gerade, straight away; handle is from hantlich, handy, deft — here as an adverb, briskly. The Weg is spelled Wäg here and Weg elsewhere, and both are left as printed.

sentences.t: Z’ Obe chunt er zu neme Schloß, do frogt er umenes Nachtlager, denn sälbesmol het me no käine Wirthshüser gha,
sentences.l: In-the evening comes he to a castle, there asks he for-a night’s-lodging, for at-that-time had one still no inns had,
sentences.i: In the evening he came to a castle, and asked there for a night’s lodging, for in those days there were as yet no inns,
sentences.n: neme = einem; “frogt er umenes Nachtlager” = fragt er um ein Nachtlager; sälbesmol = selbesmal, at that time; me = man; Wirthshüser = Wirtshäuser, with the 1857 th. The teller stops to explain the custom of the old days to his listeners — the aside is his, not ours.

sentences.t: das säit em der Herr vom Schloß mit vele Freude zue und frogt ne woner he well.
sentences.l: that says him the lord of-the castle with many joys granting and asks him where-he to wanted.
sentences.i: and the lord of the castle granted it him gladly, and asked him where he was bound.
sentences.n: “säit … zue” = sagt zu, grants, promises, with the particle zue at the end; vele Freude = vielen Freuden; “woner he well” = wo er hin wolle — he is hin, whither, and not er.

sentences.t: Der Hans git druf zur Antwort „zum Vogelgrif.“
sentences.l: The Hans gives thereupon as answer “to the Vogel Greif.”
sentences.i: Hans answered: “To the Vogel Greif.”
sentences.n: git and gitt, gives, are both used in this tale, a line apart. The answer is bare, and it is enough to set the next errand going: this is how the tale collects its three questions.

sentences.t: „So, zum Vogelgrif, me säit ame er wuß alles, und i hane Schlössel zue nere isige Gäldchiste verlore: ehr chöntet doch so guet si und ne froge woner seig.“
sentences.l: “So, to the Vogel Greif, one says always he knew everything, and I have-the key to an iron money-chest lost: you could indeed so good be and him ask where-it were.”
sentences.i: “So, to the Vogel Greif — they always say he knows everything, and I have lost the key to an iron money-chest: you might be so good as to ask him where it is.”
sentences.n: ame is the Swiss amel, always, each time — though it can also be einem, to one, and the sentence bears either. hane = habe den; Schlössel = Schlüssel; ehr = ihr, the polite you; chöntet = könntet; seig = sei. The chest is isig, of iron, the same word the manikin’s clothes were made of.

sentences.t: „Jo frile,“ säit der Hans, „das wili scho thue.“
sentences.l: “Yes indeed,” says the Hans, “that will-I readily do.”
sentences.i: “Yes indeed,” said Hans, “I shall do that willingly.”
sentences.n: frile = freilich; “das wili scho thue” = das will ich schon tun, with wili for will i — the pronoun swallowed into the verb again. thue is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: Am Morgen früe isch er do witer gange, und chunt unterwägs zue mene andere Schloß, i dem er wieder übernacht blibt.
sentences.l: In-the morning early is he then further gone, and comes on-the-way to another castle, in which he again over-night stays.
sentences.i: Early in the morning he went on, and came on the way to another castle, where he again stayed the night.
sentences.n: unterwägs = unterwegs; mene = einem; übernacht blibt = über Nacht bleibt. The second castle is built exactly like the first, and so will be the third station, the water; the tale is laying out its three questions in a row.

sentences.t: Wo d’ Lüt drus verno händ daß er zum Vogelgrif well, so säge se es sig im Hus ne Tochter chrank,
sentences.l: When the people out-of-it heard have that he to the Vogel Greif wanted, so say they there be in-the house a daughter ill,
sentences.i: When the people there heard that he was going to the Vogel Greif, they said that a daughter in the house was ill,
sentences.n: Lüt = Leute; drus = daraus; verno = vernommen; säge = sagen; sig = sei. This is the second of the three questions, and it is the one that will be answered by a toad under the cellar stairs.

sentences.t: und se hebe scho alle Mittel brucht, aber es well kais aschlo,
sentences.l: and they had already all remedies used, but it wanted none to-take-hold,
sentences.i: and they had tried every remedy already, but none would take effect,
sentences.n: brucht = gebraucht; kais = keins; aschlo = anschlagen, to take effect — said of a medicine; the particle a (an) stands in front of the infinitive here, glued to it.

sentences.t: er söll doch so guet si und der Vogelgrif froge was die Tochter wieder chön gsund mache.
sentences.l: he should indeed so good be and the Vogel Greif ask what the daughter again well make could.
sentences.i: so would he be so good as to ask the Vogel Greif what could make the daughter well again.
sentences.n: “so guet si” = so gut sein, the same courteous formula the first castle used; chön = könne. The tale’s phrasing for asking a favour is identical at both castles, and that sameness is what makes the three questions feel like a set.

sentences.t: Der Hans säit das weller gärn thue und goht witer.
sentences.l: The Hans says that would-he gladly do and goes further.
sentences.i: Hans said he would gladly do it, and went on.
sentences.n: “weller” = well er, wolle er, the pronoun swallowed into the verb; gärn = gern; goht = geht, third person singular.

sentences.t: Do chunt er zue emne Wasser, und anstatt eme Feer isch e große große Ma do gsi, de all Lüt het müesse übere träge.
sentences.l: Then comes he to a water, and instead-of a ferryman was a great great man there, who all people had had-to over carry.
sentences.i: Then he came to a stretch of water, and instead of a ferryman there was a great, great man, who had to carry everybody across.
sentences.n: emne = einem; Feer = Fährmann; Ma = Mann, not man, one; “het müesse übere träge” = hat hinüber tragen müssen. The doubled große große is the 1857 text’s own and is kept — this is a giant, and the tale says so twice rather than once.

sentences.t: De Ma het der Hans gfrogt wo si Räis ane geu.
sentences.l: The man has the Hans asked where his journey to went.
sentences.i: The man asked Hans where his journey was taking him.
sentences.n: Räis = Reise; “ane geu” = hin gehe — ane is hin, the direction away from the speaker, and it stands after the noun in the southern way.

sentences.t: „Zum Vogelgrif“ säit der Hans.
sentences.l: “To the Vogel Greif” says the Hans.
sentences.i: “To the Vogel Greif,” said Hans.
sentences.n: The same four words he gave at the castle. The tale answers its own repetitions exactly, and the reader can hear the third question coming.

sentences.t: „No, wenn er zue nme chömet,“ säit do de Ma, „sö froget ne an worum i all Lüt müeß über das Wasser träge.“
sentences.l: “Well, when you to him come,” says then the man, “so ask him about why I all people must over the water carry.”
sentences.i: “Well, when you come to him,” said the man, “ask him why I have to carry everybody over this water.”
sentences.n: er here is not er, he, but ihr, the plural you — the verb chömet, second person plural, is what gives it away, and the man is addressing Hans as ihr out of courtesy. nme = ihm; sö = so; “froget … an” = fragt an, with the particle an sitting straight after the pronoun.

sentences.t: Do säit der Hans „jo, min Gott jo, das wili scho thue.“
sentences.l: Then says the Hans “yes, my God yes, that will-I readily do.”
sentences.i: “Yes, my God, yes,” said Hans, “I shall do that willingly.”
sentences.n: min = mein. Hans promises for the third time in the same words — das wili scho thue — and the three promises are what he will have to remember at the griffin’s house.

sentences.t: De Ma het ne do uf d’ Achsle gno und übere träit.
sentences.l: The man has him then onto the shoulder taken and over carried.
sentences.i: Then the man took him on his shoulder and carried him across.
sentences.n: Achsle = Achsel, shoulder; gno = genommen; “übere träit” = hinüber getragen. The giant carrying a man across water on his shoulder is a very old picture and the tale does not stop over it.

sentences.t: Ändle chunt do der Hans zum Hus vom Vogelgrif, aber do isch nume d’ Frau dehäime gsi und der Vogelgrif sälber nid.
sentences.l: At-last comes then the Hans to-the house of-the Vogel Greif, but there was only the wife at-home been and the Vogel Greif himself not.
sentences.i: At last Hans came to the Vogel Greif’s house, but only the wife was at home, and not the Vogel Greif himself.
sentences.n: dehäime = daheim; nume = nur; sälber = selber. The griffin’s wife is the whole apparatus of the tale from here on: she asks, he answers in his sleep, and she passes the answers on.

sentences.t: Do frogt ne d’ Frau was er well.
sentences.l: Then asks him the wife what he wanted.
sentences.i: The wife asked him what he wanted.
sentences.n: well = wolle, subjunctive of the reported question, as with the manikin’s questions earlier.

sentences.t: Do het ere der Hans alles verzelt, daß ere Fädere sölt ha us s’ Vogelgrife Stehl,
sentences.l: Then has to-her the Hans everything told, that he-a feather should have out-of the Vogel Greif’s tail,
sentences.i: Then Hans told her everything: that he was to have a feather out of the Vogel Greif’s tail,
sentences.n: “daß ere Fädere sölt ha” is er e Fädere, he a feather, run together into one word — the same spelling that means ihr, to her, at the start of the sentence. sölt = sollte; “s’ Vogelgrife Stehl” = des Vogel Greifs Schweif, an old genitive without an article.

sentences.t: und denn hebe se emene Schloß der Schlüssel zue nere Gäldchiste verlore, und er sött der Vogelgrif froge wo der Schlüssel seig;
sentences.l: and then had they at-a castle the key to a money-chest lost, and he should the Vogel Greif ask where the key were;
sentences.i: and that at one castle they had lost the key to a money-chest, and he was to ask the Vogel Greif where the key was;
sentences.n: emene = in einem; sött = sollte; seig = sei. Hans now recites all three errands in one breath, and the tale sets them out as a list because they will be answered as a list.

sentences.t: denn seig eme andere Schloß e Tochter chrank, und er söt wüße was die Tochter chönt gsund mache;
sentences.l: then were at-an other castle a daughter ill, and he should know what the daughter well make could;
sentences.i: that at another castle a daughter was ill, and he was to know what could make the daughter well;
sentences.n: eme = in einem; söt = sollte, spelled a letter shorter than the sött of the line before; chönt = könnte.

sentences.t: denn seig nig wid vo do es Wasser und e Ma derbi, de d’ Lüt müeß übere träge,
sentences.l: then were not far from there a water and a man beside-it, who the people must over carry,
sentences.i: that not far from there was a stretch of water and a man beside it who had to carry people across,
sentences.n: nig = nicht; wid = weit; derbi = dabei, beside it. The third errand is repeated in the same words the ferryman used, which is how the tale keeps its three threads from tangling.

sentences.t: und er möcht au gern wüsse worum de Ma all Lüt müeß übere träge.
sentences.l: and he would also gladly know why the man all people must over carry.
sentences.i: and that he would gladly know why the man had to carry everybody across.
sentences.n: möcht = möchte; “au gern wüsse” = auch gern wissen. Hans has added a question of his own to the two he was given — and it is his own question that will make him rich.

sentences.t: Do säit die Frau „ja lueget, mi guete Fründ, s’ cha käi Christ mit em Vogelgrif rede, er frißt se all;
sentences.l: Then says the wife “yes look, my good friend, it can no Christian with the Vogel Greif speak, he devours them all;
sentences.i: Then the wife said: “Look you, my good friend, no Christian soul can speak with the Vogel Greif — he devours them all;
sentences.n: Christ here means a Christian, that is a human being as against the monster — the ogre in these tales smells Christenfleisch as the giant in English smells the blood of an Englishman, and the word is a name for humankind rather than a statement about anybody’s faith. lueget = schaut, the polite plural imperative; Fründ = Freund; frißt is the verb used of animals eating, and that is the point.

sentences.t: wenn er aber wänd, so chön neder under sis Bett undere ligge,
sentences.l: if you however want, so can you under his bed underneath lie,
sentences.i: but if you like, you can lie down under his bed,
sentences.n: wänd = wollt; “chön neder” = könnet ihr, with the pronoun swallowed by the verb; sis = sein; undere = hinunter, darunter. She is addressing him as ihr, as the ferryman did.

sentences.t: und z’ Nacht, wenn er rächt fest schloft, so chönneder denn use länge und em e Fädere usem Stehl riße;
sentences.l: and at night, when he right fast sleeps, so can-you then out reach and him a feather out-of-the tail tear;
sentences.i: and at night, when he is fast asleep, you can reach out and tear a feather out of his tail;
sentences.n: chönneder = könnt ihr; “use länge” = hinauslangen, to reach out; riße = reißen. länge here is the verb langen, to reach, not die Länge, length.

sentences.t: und wäge dene Sache, die ner wüße söttet, will i ne sälber froge.
sentences.l: and because-of those things, which you know should, will I him myself ask.
sentences.i: and as for the things you are to know, I shall ask him myself.”
sentences.n: ner = ihr, you, standing after the relative die; söttet = solltet; wäge = wegen. The 1857 printing opens this speech with a German opening quotation mark and never closes it: the closing mark simply does not come, and the text is left exactly as it stands, with the English supplying the closing mark it needs.

sentences.t: Der Hans isch e das alles z’friede gsi und lit unders Bett undere.
sentences.l: The Hans was with that all content and lies himself under-the bed underneath.
sentences.i: Hans was content with all that, and lay down under the bed.
sentences.n: “e das alles z’friede” = in dem allem zufrieden; lit = liegt, here in the sense of legt sich, lays himself down; unders = unter das.

sentences.t: Z’ Obe chunt der Vogelgrif häi, und wiener i d’ Stube chunt, so säit er „Frau, i schmöke ne Christ.“
sentences.l: In-the evening comes the Vogel Greif home, and as-he into the parlour comes, so says he “wife, I smell a Christian.”
sentences.i: In the evening the Vogel Greif came home, and as he came into the parlour he said: “Wife, I smell a Christian.”
sentences.n: schmöke is the Swiss schmöcke, which means to smell, not to taste — the false friend is worth having: High German schmecken and Swiss schmöcke have swapped senses. wiener = wie er.

sentences.t: „Jo,“ säit do d’ Frau, „s’ isch hüt äine do gsi, aber er isch wieder furt;“ und mit dem het der Vogelgrif nüt me gsäit.
sentences.l: “Yes,” says then the wife, “it has today one here been, but he is again away;” and with that has the Vogel Greif nothing more said.
sentences.i: “Yes,” said the wife, “there was one here today, but he has gone again” — and at that the Vogel Greif said no more.
sentences.n: hüt = heute; äine = einer; nüt me = nichts mehr. The wife’s lie is calm and exact: everything in it is true except the last word.

sentences.t: Z’ mitzt e der Nacht, wo der Vogelgrif rächt geschnarchlet het, so längt der Hans ufe und rißt em e Fädere usem Stehl.
sentences.l: At midst in the night, when the Vogel Greif right snored had, so reaches the Hans up and tears him a feather out-of-the tail.
sentences.i: In the middle of the night, when the Vogel Greif was snoring away, Hans reached up and tore a feather out of his tail.
sentences.n: “z’ mitzt e der Nacht” = zumitzt in der Nacht, in the middle of the night; geschnarchlet = geschnarcht; “längt … ufe” = langt hinauf; rißt = reißt.

sentences.t: Do isch der Vogelgrif plötzle ufgjuckt und säit „Frau, i schmöcke ne Christ, und s’ isch mer s’ heb me öpper am Stehl zehrt.“
sentences.l: Then is the Vogel Greif suddenly up-started and says “wife, I smell a Christian, and it is to-me it had me somebody at-the tail pulled.”
sentences.i: At that the Vogel Greif started up and said: “Wife, I smell a Christian, and it seems to me somebody has been pulling at my tail.”
sentences.n: plötzle = plötzlich; ufgjuckt = aufgejuckt, started up out of sleep; “s’ isch mer” = es ist mir, it seems to me; me = mir; öpper = jemand; zehrt = gezerrt. schmöcke here and schmöke a few lines back are the same word spelled two ways.

sentences.t: De säit d’ Frau „de hesch gwüß traumet, und i ho der jo hüt scho gsäit, s’ isch e Christ do gsi, aber isch wieder furt.
sentences.l: Then says the wife “you have surely dreamed, and I have you indeed today already said, there has a Christian here been, but is again away.
sentences.i: Then the wife said: “You have surely been dreaming. I told you today already that a Christian was here, but that he went away again.
sentences.n: de here is du, you — the pronoun worn down to a single syllable and leaning on the verb hesch, you have; der in “i ho der … gsäit” is dir, to you. ho = habe; traumet = geträumt.

sentences.t: Do het mer allerhand Sache verzellt.
sentences.l: There has to-me all-sorts-of things told.
sentences.i: He told me all sorts of things.
sentences.n: The subject is simply missing — “Do het mer allerhand Sache verzellt” has no er in it, and spoken language leaves such a pronoun out where the sense is plain. The English has to supply it. mer = mir; verzellt = erzählt.

sentences.t: Si hebe ime Schloß der Schlüssel zue nere Gäldchiste verlore und chönnene numme finde.“
sentences.l: They had at-a castle the key to a money-chest lost and could-it no-longer find.”
sentences.i: They had lost the key to a money-chest at a castle, and could not find it any more.”
sentences.n: ime = in einem; chönnene = könnten ihn, the pronoun swallowed once more; numme = nicht mehr, no longer. She feeds him the first question as gossip, and he answers it as a man scoffing at fools.

sentences.t: „O di Nare,“ säit der Vogelgrif, „de Schlüssel lit im Holzhus hinder der Thör undere Holzbig.“
sentences.l: “Oh the fools,” says the Vogel Greif, “the key lies in-the wood-house behind the door under-the wood-pile.”
sentences.i: “Oh, the fools,” said the Vogel Greif, “the key is lying in the wood-house behind the door under the woodpile.”
sentences.n: di = die; Nare = Narren; Thör = Tür with the 1857 th; Holzbig = Holzbeige, the stacked pile of firewood, a thoroughly Swiss word; undere = unter der. First answer of three, and each will be introduced by the same contempt.

sentences.t: „Und denn het er au gsäit imene Schloß seig e Tochter chrank und se wüße kais Mittel für se gsund z’ mache.“
sentences.l: “And then has he also said at-a castle were a daughter ill and they knew no remedy for her well to make.”
sentences.i: “And then he said that at a castle a daughter was ill, and they knew no remedy to make her well.”
sentences.n: imene = in einem; seig = sei; wüße = wüssten; kais = keins. The wife keeps her questions in the same shape as her gossip, so that nothing sounds like asking.

sentences.t: „O di Nare,“ säit der Vogelgrif, „under der Chällerstäge het e Chrot es Näscht gmacht von ere Hoore, und wenn se die Hoor wieder het, so wers se gsund.“
sentences.l: “Oh the fools,” says the Vogel Greif, “under the cellar-stair has a toad a nest made of her hair, and when she the hair again has, so becomes she well.”
sentences.i: “Oh, the fools,” said the Vogel Greif, “under the cellar stairs a toad has made a nest out of her hair, and when she has the hair again she will be well.”
sentences.n: Chällerstäge = Kellerstiege; Chrot = Kröte; Näscht = Nest; “von ere Hoore” = von ihrem Haar; wers = wird sie. A single hair of the sick girl’s, taken into a toad’s nest, is holding her illness — the logic is that of a charm, and the tale offers no other explanation.

sentences.t: „Und denn het er au no gsäit s’ sig amene Ort es Wasser un e Ma derbi, der müeß all Lüt drüber träge.“
sentences.l: “And then has he also still said there be at-a place a water and a man beside-it, who must all people over carry.”
sentences.i: “And he said too that at a certain place there is a water with a man beside it, who has to carry everybody across.”
sentences.n: amene Ort = an einem Ort; drüber = darüber, hinüber. The third question, put last because its answer is the one that will drown the king.

sentences.t: „O de Nar,“ säit de Vogelgrif, „täter nome emol äine z’ mitzt dri stelle, er müeßt denn käine me übere träge.“
sentences.l: “Oh the fool,” says the Vogel Greif, “did-he only once one at midst in place, he would-have then none more over to-carry.”
sentences.i: “Oh, the fool,” said the Vogel Greif, “if he would only once set somebody down in the middle of it, he would have nobody more to carry across.”
sentences.n: täter = täte er; nome = nur; “z’ mitzt dri stelle” = zumitzt hinein stellen; müeßt = müsste. The answer is a piece of cruelty offered as common sense, and the tale lets it stand without comment — as it will let the drowning stand at the end.

sentences.t: Am Morge frue isch der Vogelgrif uf gstande und isch furt gange.
sentences.l: In-the morning early is the Vogel Greif up stood and is away gone.
sentences.i: Early in the morning the Vogel Greif got up and went away.
sentences.n: frue = früh, spelled without the h it carries elsewhere in the tale; “uf gstande” = aufgestanden, printed here as two words; furt = fort.

sentences.t: Do chunt der Hans underem Bett füre und het e schöne Fädere gha;
sentences.l: Then comes the Hans from-under-the bed forth and has a fine feather had;
sentences.i: Then Hans came out from under the bed, and he had a fine feather;
sentences.n: underem = unter dem; füre = hervor, out and forward — the same spelling that was führen, to lead, earlier in the tale.

sentences.t: au het er ghört was der Vogelgrif gsäit het wäge dem Schlüssel und der Tochter und dem Ma.
sentences.l: also has he heard what the Vogel Greif said had because-of the key and the daughter and the man.
sentences.i: and he had heard what the Vogel Greif had said about the key and the daughter and the man.
sentences.n: au = auch; ghört = gehört; wäge = wegen. The three answers are counted off in the order they were asked, which is how the tale will pay them out again.

sentences.t: D’ Frau vom Vogelgrif het em do alles no nemol verzellt, daß er nüt vergäße, und denn isch er wieder häi zue gange.
sentences.l: The wife of-the Vogel Greif has him then everything once more told, so that he nothing forgot, and then is he again home-ward gone.
sentences.i: The Vogel Greif’s wife told him everything over once more, so that he should forget nothing, and then he went off home again.
sentences.n: nemol = einmal; vergäße = vergesse; “häi zue gange” = heimzu gegangen, homeward. She is the one who keeps the answers straight, and the tale gives her the credit plainly.

sentences.t: Zerst chunt er zum Ma bim Wasser, de frogt ne gli was der Vogelgrif gsäit heb,
sentences.l: First comes he to the man by-the water, who asks him at-once what the Vogel Greif said had,
sentences.i: First he came to the man by the water, who asked him at once what the Vogel Greif had said,
sentences.n: Zerst = zuerst; bim = beim; gli = gleich; heb = habe. The three stations are paid out in reverse order — the ferryman first, then the sick daughter, then the key: last asked, first answered.

sentences.t: do säit der Hans er söll ne zerst übere träge, es well em’s denn däne säge.
sentences.l: then says the Hans he should him first over carry, he-would it-him then over-there say.
sentences.i: and Hans said he should carry him across first, and he would tell him on the other side.
sentences.n: däne = drüben, over on the far side; “em’s” = ihm es. The subject of “es well em’s … säge” is the same worn-down es that stands for er elsewhere in this tale — Hans is speaking of himself in the third person, as he did to the manikin. And he is careful: he does not give the answer until he is safely across.

sentences.t: Do träit ne der Ma übere.
sentences.l: Then carries him the man over.
sentences.i: So the man carried him across.
sentences.n: Six words for the crossing, and the whole weight of the tale’s ending rests on the order of these two sentences.

sentences.t: Woner däne gsi isch, so säit em der Hans er söllt nume äinisch äine z’ mitzt dri stelle, er müeß denn käine me übere träge.
sentences.l: When-he over-there been was, so says him the Hans he should only once one at midst in place, he must then none more over carry.
sentences.i: When he was on the other side, Hans told him he need only once set somebody down in the middle, and then he would have nobody more to carry across.
sentences.n: äinisch = einmal; “z’ mitzt dri stelle” = zumitzt hinein stellen. Hans hands on the griffin’s advice exactly as he heard it, without a word about what it means — and the tale offers no comment either.

sentences.t: Do het se de Ma grüsele gfreut und säit zum Hans er well ne zum Dank none mol ume und äne trage.
sentences.l: Then has itself the man dreadfully rejoiced and says to the Hans he would him in thanks once more over and across carry.
sentences.i: At that the man was mightily pleased, and told Hans that by way of thanks he would carry him over and back once more.
sentences.n: “none mol” = noch einmal; ume und äne = hinüber und herüber, there and back. The offer is friendly and would be fatal to take up, and neither man knows it.

sentences.t: Do säit der Hans näi, er well em die Müeh erspare, er seig sust mit em z’friede, und isch witer gange.
sentences.l: Then says the Hans no, he would him the trouble spare, he were otherwise with him content, and is further gone.
sentences.i: Hans said no, he would spare him the trouble; he was well enough satisfied with him as it was — and went on his way.
sentences.n: näi = nein; Müeh = Mühe; sust = sonst; z’friede = zufrieden. Hans refuses out of courtesy, and the refusal saves his life; the tale does not say so, and does not need to.

sentences.t: Do chunt er zue dem Schloß, wo die Tochter chrank gsi isch,
sentences.l: Then comes he to the castle, where the daughter ill been was,
sentences.i: Then he came to the castle where the daughter was ill,
sentences.n: wo = wo, where, here in its plain sense and not as als. The second answer is about to be paid out.

sentences.t: die nimmt er do uf d’ Achsle, denn se het nit chönne laufe, und träit se d’ Chellerstäge ab
sentences.l: her takes he then onto the shoulder, for she had not been-able-to walk, and carries her the cellar-stair down
sentences.i: and he took her on his shoulder, for she could not walk, and carried her down the cellar stairs
sentences.n: “denn se het nit chönne laufe” = denn sie hat nicht laufen können, the double infinitive again; “träit se … ab” = trägt sie hinab. Hans carries her exactly as the giant carried him, and the tale repeats the picture on purpose.

sentences.t: und nimmt das Chrotenäst under dem underste Tritt füre und gits der Tochter i d’ Händ,
sentences.l: and takes the toad’s-nest from under the lowest step forth and gives-it to-the daughter into the hands,
sentences.i: and took the toad’s nest out from under the lowest step and put it into the daughter’s hands,
sentences.n: Chrotenäst = Krötennest; Tritt is the tread of a stair, not a form of treten; “nimmt … füre” = nimmt hervor; gits = gibt es.

sentences.t: und die springt em ab der Achsle abe und vor im d’ Stäge uf, und isch ganz gsund gsi.
sentences.l: and she springs him off the shoulder down and before him the stair up, and was quite well.
sentences.i: and she sprang down off his shoulder and up the stairs ahead of him, and was quite well.
sentences.n: abe = hinab; Stäge = Stiege, stairs; uf = hinauf. The cure is instant and unexplained, as the illness was — and the girl running up the stairs ahead of the man who carried her down is the tale’s neatest reversal.

sentences.t: Jetz händ der Vater und d’ Mueter e grüsliche Freud gha und händ dem Hans Gschänke gmacht vo Gold und Silber:
sentences.l: Now have the father and the mother a monstrous joy had and have to-the Hans presents made of gold and silver:
sentences.i: Now the father and mother were overjoyed, and made Hans presents of gold and silver:
sentences.n: grüsliche is gräulich used, like grüsele, as a sheer intensifier — a monstrous joy, meaning a very great one; Mueter = Mutter; Gschänke = Geschenke.

sentences.t: und was er nume het welle, das händ sem gge.
sentences.l: and what he only wanted, that have they-him given.
sentences.i: and whatever he wanted, they gave him.
sentences.n: “was er nume het welle” = was er nur hat haben wollen; sem = sie ihm; gge = gegeben. welle here is wollen, the past participle in a double infinitive, and not eine Welle.

sentences.t: Wo do der Hans is an der Schloß cho isch, isch er gli is Holzhus gange,
sentences.l: When then the Hans into the other castle come was, went he at-once into-the wood-house,
sentences.i: When Hans came to the other castle he went straight to the wood-house,
sentences.n: The 1857 text prints “is an der Schloß,” and the likeliest reading is ins ander Schloss, into the other castle — is for ins, an der standing for ander — which is what the sense of the errand requires; but the words are printed as they stand and the reading is not certain.

sentences.t: und het hinder der Thör under der Holzbige de Schlüssel richtig gfunde, und het ne do dem Herr brocht.
sentences.l: and has behind the door under the wood-pile the key rightly found, and has it then to-the lord brought.
sentences.i: and behind the door, under the woodpile, he did indeed find the key, and brought it to the lord of the castle.
sentences.n: richtig here is sure enough, right enough — the confirmation of what the griffin said, not the manner of the finding; gfunde = gefunden; brocht = gebracht.

sentences.t: De het se au nid wenig gfreut
sentences.l: He has himself also not a-little rejoiced
sentences.i: He too was not a little pleased,
sentences.n: De = der, and it opens the sentence as a demonstrative — that one, this man — which is how spoken German picks up the person just named.

sentences.t: und het dem Hans zur Belohnig vill vo dem Gold gge, das e der Chiste gsi isch, und sust no aller derhand für Sache, so Chüe und Schoof und Gäiße.
